findings.claim: A DAW — defined in the opening line and in the glossary as "software used to record, edit and produce music on a computer" — "is a software application for recording, editing and producing music. But the software is only part of the picture".
findings.truth: The spec glossary defines the term the other way: "the term DAW, or digital audio workstation, is used to refer to both the hardware and software elements that make up a computer-based music production environment". Content area 2.1 is titled "how hardware and software work in combination as a digital audio workstation". A student who defines a DAW as software only can lose the definition mark.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1 heading and glossary entry "Digital audio workstation (DAW)"

findings.claim: Q5 indicative content: "SSD — faster load times for samples and projects, reduces latency".
findings.truth: Drive speed does not set audio latency. Latency is set by the buffer size and the sample rate, as Lesson 2 teaches. A fast drive gives quicker loading and smoother streaming of large sample libraries. The mark scheme contradicted the next lesson.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1.2 buffer size settings (for recording / for mixing / latency); internal contradiction with L2

findings.claim: Band ladders in the 6-mark and 8-mark schemes of all three lessons end with "Lower band (1-2)".
findings.truth: House band vocabulary is Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band. "Lower band" sits next to "Lower-mid band" in the same ladder and reads as a sixth, undefined band.
findings.evidence: house band vocabulary (six places: L1 Q5/Q6, L2 Q5/Q6, L3 Q5/Q6)

findings.claim: "know the difference between EQ (frequency), dynamics (volume) and modulation (time-based) effects".
findings.truth: The spec lists reverb and delay as the time-based effects, with modulation (chorus, flanging, phasing) as a separate category. The lesson body already classifies them correctly, so the exam tip taught the opposite of its own content.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1.2 processing plug-ins: effects → time-based effects (reverb, delay); modulation effects (chorus, flanging, phasing)

findings.claim: Flashcard 13 asks "What is the advantage of a 'workstation' DAW over a cloud DAW?"
findings.truth: The spec names two types of DAW software: cloud-based and desktop applications. "Workstation DAW" is not a term in the qualification, and the card's own answer says "Desktop DAWs". Every DAW is a workstation, so the question invites confusion.

findings.claim: The hazard list gives "Displays — ... causes eye strain, headaches and fatigue" and puts back pain under slips, trips and falls: "can cause falls, resulting in back pain, sprains or fractures"; the key fact repeats "displays (eye strain), slip/trip/fall (back pain, sprains)".
findings.truth: The spec's hazard is "use of computer displays and workstations", and its risk list pairs that hazard with eye strain and back pain; slips, trips and falls carry sprains and breaks. Posture at a badly set up desk is the back-pain route the spec expects, and the lesson never mentioned posture at all.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2.2 health and safety: hazards and risks lists

findings.claim: "16 GB is a common minimum for music production."
findings.truth: No spec figure exists and manufacturers' minimums vary (8 GB is a common stated minimum for entry-level DAW use). The lesson frames it as "a common minimum", not a spec requirement, so it is defensible, but the flashcard turns it into a recall item with one right number.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1.1 names RAM without any figure

summary: All 3 lessons carry findings, none HIGH: the DAW definition contradicted the spec (software only), an SSD was credited with reducing latency, modulation was labelled time-based, and the workstation hazard was stripped of its back-pain risk. Every knowledge-check key, match order and practice tariff was recomputed and is correct, and no lesson calls this a GCSE, names a paper or invents an examiner claim.
